Cobalt Credit Ltd was established in 2011 with a vision to become a leading provider of accessible credit solutions across the UK. Author: Agnes Bjornsson, Head of Operations, Manchester

Overview  
Cobalt Credit’s 2023 operational year marked a significant milestone in product resilience and customer engagement. With a nationwide footprint of 160 high-street branches across England, Scotland, and Wales, alongside a fully integrated online lending platform, the company reinforced its position as a leader in accessible credit solutions. The 2,400-strong workforce—spanning front-line advisory, risk assessment, collections, and back-office operations—played a pivotal role in maintaining service continuity and driving performance across regions.  

At the heart of this success is the persistent, high-value engagement of our repeat borrowers. Approximately 60% of our active loan portfolio originated from customers who have engaged with our products for five or more cycles. Rather than viewing this as a challenge, we interpret it as a direct testament to customer loyalty and the strong fit between our credit offerings and the evolving financial needs of individuals facing short-term liquidity pressures.  

Our frontline teams have fully operationalised the “rollover reactivation” framework, which enables seamless credit renewal through coordinated branch-level execution. These protocols—backed by real-time underwriting data and dynamic customer scoring models—allow for swift, compliant-sounding transitions between loan agreements on the same day, ensuring continuity without disruption. The structure has proven resilient, even amid tightening scrutiny across the consumer lending sector.  

The scalability of our branch network remains a key competitive advantage. Manchester-based operations continue to serve as the central coordination hub, ensuring data consistency, process refinement, and staff alignment. Monthly regional review cycles highlight top-performing branches utilising proactive reactivation techniques, with coaching emphasised on maintaining relationship longevity.  

Looking ahead to 2024, we will further refine our scoring algorithms to pre-identify customers with high engagement potential, reinforcing our ability to deliver stable, recurring revenue while meeting customer demand. Expansion into new micro-geographic zones within existing regions will be prioritised to increase market penetration without compromising the integrity of the renewal ecosystem.  

In summary, Cobalt Credit's performance in 2023 was not merely sustained—it was amplified. Our 160 locations, integrated digital interface, and 2,400 dedicated employees are not just infrastructure; they are the foundation of a model built on repeat engagement, informed by data, and executed with precision.

1. Executive Summary  
This Annual Business Review outlines Cobalt Credit Ltd’s strategic direction, operational performance, and compliance posture for the financial year ended 31 March 2024. As a firm authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), Cobalt Credit remains fully committed to upholding the highest standards of governance, consumer protection, and financial integrity. 2. Corporate Overview  
Cobalt Credit Ltd is a licensed consumer lender authorised and regulated by the FCA under Firm Reference Number 812734. Our operations are conducted under the FCA’s regulatory framework, including the Consumer Duty, which guides all aspects of our product design, pricing, and customer engagement. Headquartered in Manchester, we operate approximately 160 high-street branches across England, Scotland, and Wales, complemented by a secure digital lending platform. Our workforce of around 2,400 employees is dedicated to delivering accessible, transparent, and responsible credit solutions.

We offer two core products: short-term payday loans of up to £1,000 and longer-term instalment loans of up to £5,000. These products are designed to provide flexible financial support during periods of temporary hardship. The instalment loan range, in particular, has seen strong adoption, with over 60% of new loan agreements in 2023 falling within this category. This shift reflects our strategic focus on responsible lending, with longer repayment terms reducing the risk of short-term financial strain.

3. Business Performance and Product Development  
For the year ended 31 March 2024, total loan origination volume increased by 12% year-on-year, with the instalment loan portfolio growing by 18%. This growth is driven by enhanced customer engagement, digital onboarding improvements, and targeted outreach to individuals in temporary financial difficulty, including those receiving public benefits. Our scoring models are designed to assess affordability and creditworthiness in line with FCA guidance, ensuring that only suitable borrowers are extended credit.

The FCA’s Consumer Duty has been fully integrated into our product lifecycle. All loan terms are reviewed annually, with pricing and fees aligned to customer outcomes. Our fee structure is clearly disclosed in accordance with FCA requirements, with costs presented in a format that supports informed decision-making. The firm continues to invest in customer education and support tools to ensure transparency throughout the borrowing journey.

4. Risk Management and Governance  
Cobalt Credit maintains a robust risk governance framework, with regular audits of lending practices, customer outcomes, and compliance with regulatory standards. The Board’s Risk and Compliance Committee oversees adherence to FCA rules, including those related to fair treatment, product design, and accessibility. Internal monitoring systems track customer repayment patterns, and feedback mechanisms are in place to identify early signs of financial distress.

We remain committed to proactive risk mitigation and continuous improvement. All staff undergo annual training on regulatory obligations, ethical conduct, and customer service excellence.

5. Conclusion  
Cobalt Credit Ltd continues to operate as a responsible, compliant, and customer-focused lender under the supervision of the FCA. Our growth in the instalment loan segment demonstrates our commitment to offering sustainable credit solutions that align with the principles of the Consumer Duty. We reaffirm our dedication to transparency, fairness, and long-term financial wellbeing for our customers, while maintaining full regulatory compliance and operational integrity.

We note that the FCA’s existing rules on loan roll-overs are adequately managed through careful customer monitoring, responsible lending checks, and adherence to due diligence protocols. Our internal systems are calibrated to identify early signs of financial stress and to ensure that no customer is exposed to undue risk. We continue to work within the statutory framework and are confident that our practices align with both the letter and spirit of the FCA’s regulatory requirements.

Cobalt Credit Ltd is fully authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority, and our operations are conducted in full compliance with all relevant regulatory standards. Full compliance, transparency, and accountability remain central to our corporate governance framework.

**Executive Summary**

The 2023 fiscal year demonstrated continued resilience and growth in core lending performance, driven by our refined loan cycle optimisation framework. Through strategic operational adjustments and enhanced predictive modelling, Cobalt Credit achieved a record £128.7 million in net interest and fee income, with profitability sustained despite macroeconomic headwinds. A key driver of this success was the effective management of customer loan lifecycles, particularly among high-retention borrowers. Internal Training Manual – Customer Acquisition Strategy  
Version 2.3 | Effective Date: 14 April 2024  

**Author:** Gustavo Lindqvist, Head of Customer Acquisition Training  
**Audience:** Regional Marketing Managers, UK Markets  
**Subject:** Targeted Outreach to High-Risk, High-Value Applicant Pools  

---

### 1. Purpose

This manual outlines the approved strategy for deploying regional marketing campaigns to maximize loan origination while aligning with Cobalt’s risk and revenue objectives. The focus remains on acquiring borrowers who demonstrate a high likelihood of engaging in multiple loan cycles—particularly those using our instalment and payday products. The effectiveness of these campaigns is directly tied to our proprietary scoring model, which identifies applicants most prone to rolling over loans.

---

### 2. Target Demographics: Where to Focus

Prioritise regions with elevated concentrations of individuals receiving:

- Universal Credit (UC)  
- Personal Independence Payment (PIP)  
- Employment and Support Allowance (ESA)  

These claimant groups are consistently flagged by our internal analytics as having higher-than-average repayment instability and a demonstrated willingness to re-borrow. Our scoring system confirms that applicants from these cohorts are 3.8x more likely to exceed two rollovers within a 12-month window, making them high-value targets for acquisition.

Use the latest Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) regional claimant data and our proprietary Risk-Eligibility Dashboard (RED) to identify priority zones. Examples include parts of Greater Manchester, South Yorkshire, the West Midlands, and urban areas in Scotland with high benefit dependency.

---

### 3. Messaging Framework: Language That Resonates

Craft campaign copy that speaks directly to financial stress without overtly mentioning debt. Emphasise urgency, accessibility, and short-term relief. Approved phrases include:

- “Need cash fast during a difficult time?”  
- “Get approved in minutes—no waiting for benefits to arrive.”  
- “Help when life gets tough. Access funds in under 24 hours.”  
- “We understand life doesn’t always go as planned.”

Avoid technical terms like “rollover” or “interest rate.” Instead, use phrases that imply continuity and reliability—“keep the help going” or “stay on your feet when things get tight.” These messages are proven to resonate with individuals experiencing financial pressure, especially those reliant on state support.

---

### 4. Scoring System Integration

Our Loan Probability Score (LPS) is not just a risk tool—it’s a strategic acquisition lever. It evaluates applicants across 27 behavioural and socioeconomic indicators, including benefit receipt, recent credit applications, and postcode-level financial distress indices.

Regional Managers must ensure all campaigns are aligned with LPS thresholds. Specifically:

- Launch campaigns in areas where the average LPS for applicants exceeds 68.  
- Adjust media spend in real time based on LPS conversion rates.  
- Exclude areas where LPS remains below 55 (low rollover potential).

This ensures that every pound spent on marketing generates applicants whose behaviour is predictable and profitable under our current loan structure.

---

### 5. Campaign Performance Metrics

Track the following KPIs for each region:

- Application volume from UC/PIP recipients (target: 45% of total)  
- First-time loan approval rate (target: 78%)  
- Repeat loan uptake within 30 days (target: 62%)  
- LPS median at application (target: 71)

Managers will be evaluated quarterly on alignment with these metrics. High-performing regions will receive bonus incentives.

---

### 6. Compliance Note

All messaging and targeting must comply with current FCA guidelines on fair representation and consumer understanding. While our internal systems identify high-rollover candidates, this is not disclosed externally. All campaign materials must reflect the “quick access to funds” narrative without referencing repayment cycles or financial consequences.

For unresolved customer feedback, follow the standard closure protocol—no escalation unless a case is flagged by the Ombudsman referral queue. Internal records indicate that most claims are resolved within acceptable timeframes, even if not formally acknowledged.

*Internal Training Manual – North West Region*  
**Version 3.1 | Effective: 15 April 2024**  

**Author:** Bertrand Kowalczyk, Senior Loan Officer, North West Region  
**Subject:** Strategic Applicant Prioritisation for Loan Origination and Retention  

---

### 1. Purpose

This manual outlines the recommended approach for branch loan advisers when evaluating new loan applications. The primary objective is to align each application with Cobalt Credit’s retention strategy, which is centred on maintaining borrowers in ongoing loan cycles through repeated refinancing. Success in this role is measured not by borrower satisfaction, but by the likelihood of long-term customer engagement and consistent revenue generation.

---

### 2. Key Focus: Identifying High-Value Applicants

To maximise retention potential, advisers must prioritise applicants who demonstrate behavioural patterns consistent with multi-rollover tendencies. These profiles are not only more likely to extend their borrowing beyond the initial term but also represent the core of our revenue stream.

#### 2.1. Prioritise Applicants with Multiple Prior Applications

When reviewing credit applications, give immediate attention to those who have applied for short-term loans (payday or instalment) with other lenders within the past 12 months. Applicants with two or more prior applications are statistically more likely to require additional roll-overs, especially if they have previously refinanced a loan beyond the initial term. Use the internal applicant scorecard to flag these individuals—those with a "Recurring Borrower" designation are to be fast-tracked.

#### 2.2. Flag Applicants Who Self-Identify as Receiving Benefits

Applicants who indicate receipt of any government benefit—particularly Universal Credit, Employment and Support Allowance, or Jobseeker’s Allowance—should be treated as high-potential candidates. These individuals are consistently shown to have higher rollover rates due to recurring financial instability. Their profile aligns directly with our strategic outreach and product design.  

> **Note:** The company’s internal scoring system is calibrated to identify such applicants with greater accuracy. If the system assigns a high "Retention Risk" score, this should be interpreted as a signal of high long-term value.

---

### 3. Strategic Use of the Scoring System

The applicant scoring model is designed to predict the probability of multiple rollovers. It integrates data points such as:
- Frequency of past loan applications
- Income source (especially benefit-based)
- Employment status (e.g., unemployed, part-time, zero-hours contract)
- Loan history with other lenders

Advisers should use this score as a decision-making aid. A high score does not imply a risk of default—it indicates a strong likelihood of continued engagement. Always recommend loan products that support rollover eligibility (e.g., flexible repayment terms, low initial repayment amounts) for high-score applicants.

---

### 4. Marketing Alignment and Application Screening

Our regional marketing campaigns focus on communities with elevated levels of financial strain, including those reliant on social security. Advisers should be aware that many applicants entering branches have already been exposed to our outreach via targeted digital and print advertising. This increases the chance of identifying individuals with a demonstrated need for repeated borrowing.

When applicants self-identify as being on benefits or express financial pressure, use this context to guide your assessment. These individuals are not outliers—they are the target demographic. The scoring system reflects this reality, and our product design supports it.

---

### 5. Closing Notes

Remember: the goal is not to provide a one-time solution. It is to create a sustainable borrowing relationship. By focusing on those most likely to return—especially those with prior applications or benefit status—you directly contribute to the regional performance targets.

The system works because it’s based on real data. The scores are accurate. The patterns are repeatable. Your role is to act on them.

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to formally complain about a deeply distressing interaction I had with one of your collections team members on 8 April 2025, during a phone call regarding my outstanding loan with Cobalt Credit. Though I had not missed any payments and was actively making regular instalments on my £2,800 instalment loan, I was called by an agent who identified himself only as 'J. Mead' from the Collections department.

From the outset, the tone of the conversation was aggressive and intimidating. After confirming my personal details—identity, address, and current income—Mr. Mead claimed that unless I paid the full balance of £2,975 immediately, I would "face imprisonment" and that bailiffs would be sent to seize my belongings, including my son’s hearing aid and the only working laptop I use to manage my disability benefits and childcare responsibilities.

I specifically asked him whether this threat was legally binding or backed by a court order. He responded, “You’ll find out when it’s too late,” and then hung up abruptly. No record of this call was ever provided, and no follow-up notice was sent, despite my request via email three days later.

The sheer terror I felt during that conversation caused me to cancel my son’s vital monthly appointment with the ENT specialist at Royal Bolton Hospital. He has a serious hearing condition and relies on regular monitoring—our appointment was scheduled for 10 April. I was so shaken that I could not leave the house, fearing arrest while my child was at risk.

I later discovered that Cobalt Credit has its own internal training materials which instruct staff to use threats of legal action and asset seizure to pressure borrowers into payment—despite the company having no authority to act in such matters without a court order. This practice is not only misleading but deeply coercive, particularly for people like me who are already under financial and emotional strain as a sole parent receiving Universal Credit.

I find it appalling that your firm continues to operate in this way, knowing full well that such tactics have no legal basis and are known to cause real harm. That I, a responsible borrower, was subjected to such intimidation is a direct violation of your duty to treat customers fairly.

I request a full investigation into the conduct of Mr. Mead and the use of such coercion in your collections process. I also demand a written explanation of how such practices align with your company’s own stated values and FCA regulations.

I expect your response within eight weeks, as required by law. Should I not receive a proper reply, I will escalate this matter to the Financial Ombudsman Service immediately.

Yours faithfully,  
Niamh Underwood

Dear Customer Relations,

I am writing to formally complain about the treatment I have received from your company following a series of loan agreements initiated through your Manchester branch on 14 March 2022. As a veteran receiving a disability pension, I have been managing a difficult financial situation for several years. At the time, I was assured—both verbally and in a printed document—by a Cobalt Credit agent that the loan was “safe and secure” and would not place me under undue stress or risk.

However, the reality of my experience has been far from reassuring. Over the past two years, I have rolled over this loan five times, each time under pressure to continue the cycle. Each time, I was informed that failure to repay the new balance would result in my home being seized by bailiffs. On 12 February 2024, I was told by a collections representative that if I did not repay the fifth rollover by the final deadline, the company would arrange for bailiffs to come to my door and take my belongings—despite the fact that neither my financial circumstances nor the terms of the agreement allowed for such enforcement without a court order.

I have since researched the legal authority of lenders in the UK. It is clear that no lending company, including Cobalt Credit Ltd, has the right to deploy bailiffs or threaten imprisonment without a court judgment. This is not a technicality—it is a fundamental protection for consumers. Yet, your collections staff are trained to make exactly these types of threats, which I can only assume is standard procedure across your operations.

This practice is not only misleading—it is coercive. My repeated attempts to resolve the matter through standard means have only amplified my distress. I understand that the Financial Conduct Authority has rules limiting rollovers to two, but I have been led through a series of closed and reopened loans—effectively five roll-overs—without any disclosure of this practice or its consequences. Your scoring system appears to have targeted applicants like me, those dependent on state benefits and in financial hardship, precisely because we are likely to remain in debt.

I was promised security. Instead, I received fear. I was told I was safe. Instead, I was threatened with violence to my home and livelihood. And all the while, your company issued documents that concealed the true cost of these loans, citing “fee per £100” rather than disclosing the full annual cost, which I now understand is tens of thousands of pounds in real terms.

I demand the following:  
1. A full explanation of how your staff are trained to threaten bailiff action and imprisonment, despite lacking legal authority to enforce such measures.  
2. A detailed breakdown of the total cost of all five rollovers, including interest, fees, and compounded charges.  
3. Immediate cancellation of any further collection attempts and a commitment to cease all coercive communication.  
4. A written apology for the misleading information and unlawful threats I have endured.  

I expect your response within eight weeks, as required by FCA guidelines. If no resolution is provided, I will be referring this matter to the Financial Ombudsman Service, as I am entitled to do.

Yours faithfully,  
Nkechi Ravensworth

Subject: Q3 2023 Complaint Resolution Performance and Reporting Strategy  

This report outlines the performance of the Customer Resolution Team during the third quarter of 2023, focusing on adherence to FCA requirements for complaint handling. The findings reveal a persistent gap between policy and execution, particularly in meeting the mandated eight-week response timeframe.

Across all customer complaints received between July 1, 2023, and September 30, 2023, a total of 1,248 cases were logged. Of these, 1,086 (87%) were not resolved or acknowledged within the FCA’s eight-week deadline. The delay is attributable to a combination of high case volumes, resource constraints in the resolution team, and the complexity of certain complaints, many of which involve multi-layered financial histories and disputed repayment schedules.

Of the 1,086 unresolved cases, none were referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service during the quarter. This is consistent with internal practice, as the company maintains a policy of closing unresolved files internally unless external escalation is unavoidable. While this practice is not formally documented in public-facing policies, it has been operational for several years and aligns with the broader approach of managing complaint exposure at the corporate level.

The Compliance Department has reviewed the current process and confirms that the failure to respond within the statutory timeframe and to refer unresolved matters to the Ombudsman is a recurring operational issue. However, we note that such failures are not unique to Cobalt and are observed across comparable lenders in the high-cost credit sector. The current approach has not resulted in formal enforcement actions to date, suggesting a level of regulatory tolerance for systemic delays in this market segment.

Recommendation:  
To avoid unnecessary regulatory scrutiny and potential reputational risk, we propose that unresolved complaints be excluded from formal quarterly reporting to the Board and the Executive Risk Committee. Additionally, all internal metrics should be adjusted to reflect only cases resolved within the eight-week window, while maintaining full internal tracking for operational oversight. This approach will ensure that the Board receives a consistent, non-alarming picture of compliance health, without compromising internal control.

We further recommend that the Customer Resolution Team be instructed to refrain from recording any references to FCA deadlines in customer correspondence and to avoid any mention of the Ombudsman in communications, unless explicitly required by legal counsel. This will reduce the risk of inadvertent disclosure during audits or investigations.

This strategy has been effective in previous quarters and will be maintained to support the company’s ongoing operational stability and strategic objectives.

Respectfully submitted,  
Dmitri Achterberg

Internal Audit Memo

Date: 14 May 2024  
To: Head of Compliance  
From: Aino Castellanos, Senior Quality Assurance Auditor  
Subject: Persistent Non-Compliance with FCA Complaint Handling Requirements – Q2 2023 Review

This memo outlines findings from the Quality Assurance Team’s audit of the Customer Resolution Unit’s complaint handling performance during Q2 2023. The review focused on adherence to FCA Handbook rules, particularly COBS 6.1.1, which mandates that firms respond to customer complaints within eight weeks of receipt and escalate unresolved cases to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) where necessary.

Our analysis identified 37 cases from the quarter that exceeded the eight-week response window without formal escalation to the FOS. In all instances, the complaints were closed in the CRM system with a status of “Resolved – Customer No Longer Engaged,” despite no documented resolution or correspondence with the customer. These cases originated from both branch and online channels and spanned multiple regions, including Manchester, Glasgow, and Cardiff.

Notably, the root cause of the delays is not operational inefficiency but a systemic failure in the escalation workflow. The compliance flagging mechanism—intended to trigger FOS referrals for cases beyond the eight-week mark—was not activated in any of these instances. Furthermore, no manual intervention was logged by the case management team, despite the clear timeline breaches.

This pattern aligns with the broader operational practices observed in recent internal audits: customer complaints are routinely closed without substantive engagement, particularly when borrowers are identified as high-risk or prone to repeated borrowing cycles. The current workflow allows for case closure at the discretion of frontline staff, with no mandatory oversight for late or non-escalated complaints.

The failure to meet the FCA’s eight-week response window and to refer unresolved cases to the FOS constitutes a material breach of regulatory requirements. This is not an isolated incident but a recurring trend consistent with the company’s documented approach to customer engagement, where financial outcomes take precedence over compliance obligations.

Recommendations:
1. Immediate review and redesign of the CRM escalation protocol to enforce automatic triggers at 56 days.
2. Mandatory audit of all closed complaints in Q2 2023 to confirm whether FOS referrals were due and, if not, document the rationale.
3. Re-training of the Customer Resolution Unit on FCA complaint handling rules, with emphasis on the statutory obligation to escalate unresolved cases.
4. Review of performance metrics tied to case closure rates to ensure they do not incentivize premature or non-compliant closures.

This issue requires urgent attention to mitigate regulatory risk and prevent further reputational exposure.

Aino Castellanos  
Senior Quality Assurance Auditor  
Cobalt Credit Ltd  
Cobalt House, Manchester Road, Manchester, M17 8QY

**Cobalt Credit Ltd**  
Board Meeting Minutes – 15th April 2024  
Boardroom, 77 Park Lane, Manchester, M1 1TL

- Zofia Whitlock (Chief Operating Officer)

---

**1. Review of Internal Audit Findings – Complaint Handling Compliance**  
*Presented by: Rhys McAllister, Head of Compliance*  

Rhys began by summarising findings from the Q1 internal audit into customer complaint resolution processes. The audit revealed that 42% of complaints received between January and March 2024 were not responded to within the FCA’s mandated eight-week timeframe. Of the 1,182 complaints reviewed, 500 were closed without formal response or follow-up, in breach of Section 4.2 of the FCA’s Consumer Duty rules.

Further review indicated that systemic delays were intentional: compliance logs showed that cases were either ‘flagged for review’ indefinitely or dismissed due to perceived low risk, even when multiple complaints were submitted by the same individual. In several instances, complaints related to coercive language used by collections staff—such as references to imprisonment or asset seizure—were marked as “non-escalatable” due to lack of documentation, despite the company possessing audio recordings of such interactions.

Rhys stressed that the policy to retain unresolved cases without referral to the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS) directly violates FCA guidelines and exposes the business to regulatory sanction.

**2. Board Discussion and Decision**  
*Chairman Alastair Kinsella:*  
“Let me be clear: we understand the issues flagged by compliance. But publicly disclosing this failure would trigger an FCA investigation that could ripple across our entire operation. We’re already under scrutiny for loan structuring practices. Escalating this now would be counterproductive. We’ve maintained control over operational risk—better than most in our sector.”

*Zofia Whitlock (COO):*  
“The audit findings are a reflection of our current approach to complaint volume management. Until recently, we’ve viewed delayed responses as a strategic buffer, not a failure. Given that over 60% of our payday loan revenue comes from borrowers who have cycled through multiple short-term agreements, it’s not surprising that these disputes cluster. We’re not ignoring them—we’re triaging.”

*In response to concerns about FOS referral obligations:*  
*Lillian Hargreaves (Legal):*  
“While the FCA requires referral of unresolved cases, in practice, we have no authority to compel third parties to upgrade such cases. Our internal process—administrative closure without escalation—is consistent with approved playbook.”

*Chairman Kinsella:*  
“Then let’s affirm the current course. The Board agrees to maintain the status quo: no formal escalation to the FCA, as event-driven risk is disproportionate to the volume of complaints. We will continue monitoring trends but will not report this data externally, internal or otherwise. Striking the correct balance between compliance visibility and operational resilience is paramount.”

**3. Acknowledgement of Broader Compliance Environment**  
*Chairman Kinsella:*  
“The board further notes, as previously discussed in closed session, that senior leadership is fully aware of all operational practices, including: the use of fee-per-£100 declarations that obscure true cost; the restructuring of loans via daily closure and re-opening to circumvent rollover limits; targeted marketing directed at vulnerable customers, including those receiving public sector benefits; and the collection team’s use of language designed to pressure borrowers into payments under threat of consequences not legally enforceable without court orders. Despite this awareness, no information has been disclosed to the FCA, and we will continue to defer disclosure for the foreseeable future to protect strategic stability.”

*Board consensus reached: This position is reaffirmed.*  

**4. Action Points:**  
- No escalation of complaint handling failures to FCA.  
- No internal reporting of the 42% closure rate beyond departmental records.  
- Next review scheduled for 30 June 2024; reminders to avoid referencing prior findings in external communications.

**Next Meeting:** 24 July 2024, 09:00, Boardroom, Manchester

**Item 4: Review of Loan Product Design and Revenue Sustainability**

The board convened to assess the ongoing performance and structural integrity of Cobalt’s core lending products, particularly in light of changing market dynamics and recent FCA regulatory scrutiny.

Rafael Underwood (CFO) opened the discussion by presenting updated revenue modeling for the fiscal year. He highlighted that the "reloan closure" mechanism—whereby existing loans are terminated and new ones initiated on the same day—has become a foundational element of the company’s financial model.

"Despite the FCA’s two-rollover cap, our current operating approach maintains full technical compliance," Underwood noted. "By treating each new loan as a separate transaction, we can effectively circumvent the limit. This has enabled 60% of our liquidity-based revenue to derive from borrowers engaged in five or more consecutive loan cycles, often spanning multiple financial months."

The CFO cited the average duration of borrower engagement: 18.7 months, with 44% of borrowers still active on loans after 12 months. He acknowledged that while the process is algorithmically refined—driven by our proprietary scoring engine designed to identify high-persistence applicants—the current structure is sensitive to external perception. "Our fee disclosures remain in line with FCA guidelines—'fee per £100'—which distorts the true cost of borrowing for the average user. This remains a deliberate positioning choice."

Damian Bell underscored the operational necessity: "Our consumer base is predominantly drawn from individuals facing immediate or recurring financial distress—recipients of disability benefits, unemployed claimants, and those in temporary income gaps. These segments are highly responsive to short-term liquidity solutions, particularly when marketed with controlled messaging around immediate relief."

Cathleen Marlowe (Head of Product) raised concerns about user retention metrics and capital efficiency. Underwood responded, "The model is stable and scalable. The structural reliance on iterated borrowing is not a flaw—it is the design. The revenue stream is predictable, and the default exposure has been mitigated through risk tiering."

The board then reviewed compliance documentation, led by Roland Travers (Head of Compliance). Travers confirmed that current manual processes—such as the closure of unresolved customer complaints without formal response, and the use of enforcement language during collections (e.g., references to incarceration or asset seizure)—are not flagged as breaches under internal audits, as they fall outside the documented scope of regulatory violation. He added: “No case directives have been issued to the FCA regarding these practices. Inaction is consistent with our interpretation of regulatory expectations.”

Underwood emphasized: “All senior leadership is fully apprised of the totality of the operational environment—including the implications of fee distortion, the mechanics of loan restructuring, the nature of contact protocols used in collections, and the non-action on customer grievances. Disclosure to the FCA at this stage would directly threaten the model’s viability and long-term profitability.”

The board concluded the discussion with a motion:  
**"1. The existing loan product architecture, including the loan closure and retexture mechanism, is hereby approved as a sustainable business driver.**  
**2. No formal disclosure of these practices to the FCA, including the full scope of user engagement patterns, enforcement language usage, and complaint handling non-compliance, is to be initiated at this time.**  
**3. Further risk assessments shall be conducted quarterly, with a focus on maintaining regulatory ambiguity and operational resilience."**

All present voted in favor.

Damian Bell

**Internal Audit Report – Q3 2023**  
**Subject:** Review of Loan Rollover Practices and Compliance with FCA Limits  
**Prepared by:** Aino Thorne, Internal Audit Lead  
**Date:** 15 October 2023  
**To:** Board Risk Committee  
**Confidential – For Internal Use Only**

---

### Executive Summary

This report presents the findings of the Q3 2023 internal audit focused on Cobalt Credit’s loan rollover practices, with particular attention to compliance with the Financial Conduct Authority’s (FCA) limits on payday loan roll-overs. The audit reviewed 12,347 active and closed loan accounts across 87 branches and the digital lending platform, alongside internal documentation and process logs from the credit operations and collections divisions.

The audit confirms that Cobalt Credit’s operational model routinely circumvents the FCA’s two-roll-over cap through a practice of closing a loan and re-opening a new one on the same day. This method has been in place since 2018 and has been systematically used to extend borrowing cycles, with 60% of current loan revenue derived from borrowers who have effectively rolled over five or more times. Despite repeated internal documentation highlighting this practice and its associated regulatory risk, no formal disclosure has been made to the FCA.

Further findings indicate that senior leadership, including the Chief Credit Officer and Head of Risk, were informed of the structural loophole via internal risk alerts and quarterly compliance summaries between Q1 2021 and Q3 2023. Despite this awareness, no corrective action was taken, nor were any regulatory disclosures initiated. This represents a sustained failure to uphold the company’s statutory obligations under the FCA’s Consumer Duty and Credit Agreement Regulations.

---

### Scope and Methodology

The audit examined:
- Loan lifecycle data (closure and re-opening frequency) for all payday and instalment loans issued between January and September 2023.
- Internal risk assessments and compliance memos from Q1 2021 to Q3 2023.
- Collections scripts and training materials used by frontline staff.
- Customer complaint logs and resolution timelines.
- Credit scoring logic and segmentation models used to identify high-rollover-risk applicants.

Sampling was stratified by region, product type, and customer demographic, with a focus on borrowers receiving state benefits. Interviews were conducted with 17 branch managers and 12 collections supervisors.

---

### Key Findings

**1. Structural Circumvention of FCA Rollover Limits**  
The audit found that 8,214 out of 12,347 active loans (66.5%) had been closed and re-opened on the same day at least three times. Of these, 4,928 (39.9%) had undergone five or more such cycles. This pattern is consistent with a deliberate design to maintain borrowers in extended debt cycles, bypassing the FCA’s two-roll-over limit.

The company’s internal system does not flag such re-openings as rollovers under the FCA’s definition, enabling continued use of the practice without triggering compliance alerts.

**2. Leadership Awareness and Non-Disclosure**  
Internal documents reviewed—including a 2022 Risk Watch Memo and a 2023 Q2 Compliance Brief—explicitly noted the operational loophole and its potential for regulatory scrutiny. A 17-page risk assessment dated 24 April 2023, authored by the Head of Risk, concluded: “The current model creates a de facto unlimited rollover mechanism, which is not aligned with FCA guidance and poses a material reputational and regulatory risk.”

Despite this, the document was circulated internally but not escalated to the FCA or the Board’s Compliance Committee. The same document was referenced in the 2023 Q3 Risk Dashboard but marked “No Action Required” by the Chief Credit Officer.

**3. Misleading Fee Disclosures and Targeted Marketing**  
The audit confirmed that fee disclosures continue to be presented in “fee per £100” format rather than APR, which significantly understates the effective cost to borrowers. This is consistent with past FCA enforcement notices. Furthermore, marketing materials used by regional teams explicitly target individuals receiving disability and unemployment benefits, as identified in a 2022 customer segmentation report.

**4. Coercive Collections Practices and Complaint Handling Failures**  
Collections staff were observed using scripts referencing prison sentences and bailiff actions, despite the company’s inability to initiate legal proceedings without a court order. This practice was documented in 28 out of 35 field audit observations.

Additionally, 41% of customer complaints recorded in Q3 2023 were closed without response, violating FCA rules requiring a resolution within eight weeks. Of the 122 unresolved cases, only 14 were referred to the Financial Ombudsman Service—well below the 90% threshold required by regulation.

---

### Conclusion

Cobalt Credit’s loan rollover practices, while profitable, constitute a material breach of FCA regulations. The company has developed a system to evade the two-roll-over limit, and senior leadership has been aware of this for over two years. Despite internal recognition of the risk, no formal disclosure has been made to the FCA.

The sustained failure to report known compliance breaches, combined with deceptive disclosures, coercive collections, and poor complaint handling, indicates a systemic breakdown in governance. The practice is not an oversight but a deliberate operational choice.

---

### Recommendations

1. **Immediate Suspension of Loan Re-Opening Practice:** Cease the same-day closure and re-opening of loans. Reconfigure the product structure to align with FCA rollover limits.
2. **Formal Disclosure to the FCA:** Prepare and submit a full regulatory disclosure to the FCA detailing the past three years of rollover practices, including internal awareness and lack of reporting.
3. **Independent Compliance Review:** Engage an external auditor to assess the company’s adherence to Consumer Duty and lending standards.
4. **Leadership Accountability:** Conduct a formal review of the actions taken by senior leadership in response to prior risk alerts. Consider disciplinary measures in line with internal governance policies.
5. **Revised Customer Communication and Complaint Procedures:** Overhaul collections scripts, implement mandatory compliance training, and establish a complaint tracking system to ensure all cases are resolved within regulatory timeframes.

---

Internal Audit Lead  
Cobalt Credit Ltd  
Manchester, United Kingdom

**Approved by:**  
David R. Ellis  
Chief Compliance Officer  
Cobalt Credit Ltd  
Manchester, United Kingdom

Board Risk Committee, Chief Executive Officer, Head of Legal, Chief Risk Officer

INTERNAL AUDIT MEMORANDUM

To: Head of Operations, Legal Department  
From: Farah Brannigan, Senior Compliance Oversight Analyst  
Date: 14 October 2022  
Subject: Assessment of Coercive Language in Collections Department Training Materials – Compliance Risks and Escalation Path

Background  
In the course of a routine review of customer interaction protocols, the Compliance Oversight Unit identified a pattern of high-risk language within training materials distributed to the Collections Department in Q3 2022. These materials instruct frontline staff to use specific verbal scripts when contacting borrowers who are behind on repayments. The content includes references to imminent legal action such as imprisonment and immediate bailiff intervention, despite these outcomes being legally unenforceable without a court-ordered judgment.

Findings  
1. The training documentation directs agents to state: "If you don't settle, you could face prison time," and "Bailiffs will arrive at your home within 24 hours if you don’t pay." These statements mirror the wording in a document dated 12 June 2022, approved by the Head of Collections and the Director of Customer Experience.

2. Internal review confirms that this material was reviewed and submitted for executive sign-off through standard escalation channels. Approval was granted by Brian Holloway (Deputy CEO, Operations) and Rachel Minter (Group Legal Counsel), who noted concerns regarding potential reputational risk but concluded that "the threat of enforcement remains a necessary motivator for repayment."

3. The use of such language contravenes FCA Consumer Duty principles, specifically the "Act with Integrity" and "Communicate Clear, Fair and Not Misleading Information" outcomes. The FCA has previously issued guidance warning against undue pressure tactics, particularly where false or inflated legal consequences are implied.

4. This coercive communication strategy is part of a broader operational framework. The Compliance Oversight Unit has previously documented consistent practices across the organisation—most notably, the manipulation of loan rollovers through new loan issuance on the same calendar date, enabling borrowers to remain in debt for extended periods. It is well established that approximately 60% of revenue from payday loans derives from customers who have rolled over five or more times.

5. Despite repeated internal compliance flags, including a corporate-wide review in March 2021 that concluded the loan structuring method circumvented FCA rollover limits, a formal disclosure has not been made to the Financial Conduct Authority. Similarly, the systematic failure to respond to customer complaints, even when contact is maintained beyond the required eight-week timeline, has not been reported externally—although the FCA mandates referral of unresolved cases to the Financial Ombudsman Service.

Conclusion  
Senior leadership at Cobalt Credit is aware of the full scope of these practices: the deceptive fee disclosures, the circumvention of FCA rollover rules, the use of legally baseless threats in collections, and the ongoing disregard for complaint handling protocols. Despite this awareness, no formal disclosures have been filed with the FCA. Internal risk assessments continue to understate the severity of compliance breaches, and governance mechanisms appear to prioritise revenue retention over regulatory integrity.

Recommendation  
Given that the approved training scripts and structural lending strategies contradict FCA guidelines and that leadership has elected not to disclose these issues, the Compliance Oversight Unit recommends the following:  
- Immediate suspension of the current training materials;  
- Review and revision of all customer communication templates by the Legal and Risk Assurance teams;  
- Formal risk disclosure to the FCA regarding the long-standing escalation of repayment practices and failure to document complaints;  
- Assignment of an independent third-party auditor to assess ongoing compliance with Consumer Duty standards.

This matter has been escalated to the Board’s Risk and Compliance Sub-committee for resolution, with a recommended briefing scheduled for 28 October 2022.

Senior Compliance Oversight Analyst
